content.text:
You're right to push back: my reason was effort, not fit, and you've ruled effort out. The specification set does apply to your project, so using its names and aiming for conformance is reasonable. There are two catches. Each new name has to match what the file holds. And conformance would change five parts of how your system works, so those five changes are what you'd really be deciding.

**Your three renames**
- **`REQUIREMENTS.md` → stakeholder requirements specification (StRS): fits well.** The standard separates stakeholder *needs* (raw, often vague) from stakeholder *requirements* (precisely worded). So the human-written top of your tree would be needs, and the shared levels below would be requirements. You'd fold in the business requirements specification, which 29148 allows. You'd also add operational scenarios, which it requires.
- **`CONTRACT.md` → system requirements specification (SyRS): this changes what the file is, not just its name.** An SyRS describes the whole system from outside: what it does, how well, its interfaces, constraints and assumptions, how each is checked, and links back to the stakeholder requirements. Your contract covers only the interface part. To make the name true, the bottom of your tree would split:
  - outcomes in the human's terms stay in the StRS;
  - exact system behaviours move into the SyRS.

  "Narrow" would then apply to the interface section, not the whole file. An SyRS also usually describes the system's major parts, so keeping it free of architecture (one of #3's pending changes) means describing the system as a single box.
- **Implementation → architecture and design: I'd keep "implementation" for the code.** That's the name ISO/IEC/IEEE 15288, the standard 29148 builds on, gives the stage that builds it. Architecture and design produce *descriptions*. Those would be useful as agent-owned documents next to the code, and a natural home for decision records. But they're defined in other standards (for architecture, ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010), so 29148 neither requires nor covers them.

**What conformance would change**
1. **The contract gets linked to the requirements.** Every system requirement must trace to a stakeholder requirement. That reverses #2's rule that contract lines don't cite IDs, which the scaffolds already dropped.
2. **ALWAYS/NEVER become requirements.** 29148 calls them design constraints and puts them in the SyRS. `STEERING.md` can stay its own file, because a specification can be split across files. But your rule that requirements never name a technology would need an exception for them. FAVOR/DISFAVOR and CONSIDER fit the standard's non-binding "should" and "may" wording.
3. **The kind of solution is picked first.** The first stage (business or mission analysis) chooses the kind of solution before the stakeholder requirements are written, normally on the buyer's side, which here means the human. Today your agent chooses after the requirements, based on them.
4. **Some requirements become agent-owned, if you use the recursion.** Each part's requirements would come from the agent's architecture. So "requirements are human-owned or shared" would hold only for the system as a whole. That's normal in 29148: one level's design is the next level's requirements.
5. **Every requirement must meet its writing rules:** checkable, one thing per requirement, no vague words.

It also forces a choice you haven't made: is the system the configured PC, or the setup tool? Your requirements describe the PC, while your contract describes the tool.

**Full or tailored conformance**
- **Full:** the three requirements stages, its rules for writing requirements, and the business, stakeholder and system specs. Add a software spec if you also follow the software standard (12207), though one file can serve as both. Then the operational concept document, every required section, and nothing removed.
- **Tailored** (its Annex C): you remove sections that don't apply and record why. That's how standards like this are usually applied, so it's the more useful skill to practise. I'd aim for tailored.
- **The number of files barely changes**, because 29148 lets you combine documents:
  - the StRS, combined with the business spec;
  - the SyRS, combined with the operational concept;
  - `STEERING.md` as a separate part of the SyRS;
  - the agent's design descriptions and the code.

**Two constraints that don't block it**
- **The agent has no place among 29148's roles.** It would count as a tool, which is fine: conformance needs the human to approve each document, not to have written it.
- **The standard is paywalled and your repo is public.** Your files can follow its outlines and terms, but agents can't read it, so `CONTRIBUTING.md` has to spell out its rules in your own words. Also say you follow the 2018 edition, since a new one is in progress.

These renames change the files that #2 defines, so the comment probably belongs on #2, with #3 following. I can draft it with a file-by-file mapping if you'd like.

The BSI Standards Development Portal is where draft standards open for public comment are published, and you generally need a free account to comment on them.

- **Access and registration:** BSI's portal says you register by following on-screen instructions, and then you log in to read and comment on proposed and draft standards. An existing BSI Knowledge, BSOL, or Compliance Navigator login also works.
- **Full text:** BSI's "About" page says drafts are made available for anyone to view and comment (Public comment stage). Another BSI page says the full draft can be read on its draft review system. The sources don't say clearly whether reading the full text requires a login, so check the portal directly.
- **Commenting:** Comments go on the standard's profile page. For draft standards, the portal uses a 'Comment on this section' field for comments and a 'Proposed changes' field for suggested improvements.
- **Alternative:** If submitting online is difficult, BSI says you can use a commenting template and email it to admin.start@bsigroup.com.

content.text:
No, the draft doesn't change what I'd have you build, but it does change when and how you'd claim conformance. Everything your plan relies on is still in the draft, almost all under the same names, and most visible changes make the plan simpler. The remaining risk is in the conformance rules themselves, which the preview doesn't show.

**Still there, so safe to build on now**
- The three requirements stages (business or mission analysis, stakeholder needs and requirements, system requirements), and iteration and recursion.
- The business, stakeholder and system requirements specifications, and the operational concept (OpsCon).
- The quality checklist for requirements, plus attributes and traceability.
- Stakeholder needs and system constraints as sources of requirements, now in their own section. So `ALWAYS`/`NEVER` would still count as requirements.

**Changes that affect the plan**
- **No separate software requirements spec.** Its content moves into the system requirements spec. My suggestion of one file serving as both is now how the standard works.
- **Process rename:** "architecture definition" becomes "system architecture definition". Use the new name for the agent-owned stage.
- **"Allocated requirements" now have a name.** These are the requirements the agent's architecture hands down to each part, which I said would be agent-owned if you use the recursion.
- **The writing rules look set to become guidance.** In 2018 they were part of full conformance. The draft moves them into an annex that is guidance, not rules, while the quality checklist gets its own clause of rules. Anything written to the 2018 rules still fits.
- **The concept of operations (ConOps)** moves from a guidance annex into the main list of documents, next to the OpsCon.
- **New sections on forms of requirements and on AI.** The forms section covers backlog items, models, and scenarios and use cases, so the contract could be written as scenarios. AI is listed among the tools that support requirements work, which matches treating the agent as a tool.
- **Most clause numbers change.** For example, the processes move from clause 6 to 7. So in your files, cite sections by name rather than number.

**What the preview can't tell you**
- **How tailoring works.** In 2018, Annex C held the tailoring rules I pointed you to. In the draft, Annex C is "Conformance background and options", which is guidance, and the rules are gathered into a new clause 6. A conformance claim depends on exactly these parts.
- **Which documents are required, and whether they can still be combined**, for example whether the ConOps is required, or whether the business and stakeholder specs can still be one file. The foreword's aim of producing documents from requirements models, plus a new catalogue of their content, hints at more flexibility, not less.
- **What the AI section says.**

**Revised recommendation**
1. **Go ahead with the restructure, using only what both editions share:** the stakeholder spec (with the business spec), the system spec (with the OpsCon), steering as the system spec's constraints, and "implementation" for the code.
2. **Hold off on claiming conformance and on writing tailoring records.** You can't claim conformance to a draft, and the 2018 tailoring route is changing. Do this step against the third edition once it's published.
3. **When it's out, read the conformance clause, clause 6, Annex C, the information-items overview and the AI section first.**

Voting on the draft closes 7 December 2026, so publication will probably come in 2027. Drafts at this stage usually keep their structure, but details can still change through the comments. Your later projects will use the new edition, so practising conformance against it is worth more than practising against 2018.

You may also be able to read the full draft for free. BSI says drafts open for public comment can be viewed and commented on through its Standards Development portal, and this one is open until 7 November. If the full text is there, it would answer the three open questions above, and you could comment on the AI section.

Sources:
- [BSI: Have your say on standards – a guide to public consultations](https://www.bsigroup.com/en-GB/insights-and-media/insights/blogs/have-your-say-on-standards-a-guide-to-public-consultations/)
- [BSI Standards Development portal: About](https://standardsdevelopment.bsigroup.com/Home/About)
